subjects.displayTitle: Greatness and influence of the Cause and of this Day
subjects.introduction: Bahá’u’lláh calls this the Day of God, the Day every Prophet announced and yearned to see: land and sea rejoice at its coming, the Burning Bush speaks again, and the portals of reunion stand open. Such a claim asks to be entered, not admired from a distance. He also warns that the very greatness of the Cause can become a veil, and that no mind has yet reached its root, so wonder must travel with humility, much as Isaiah sets the majesty of the Lord beside the humbling of human pride and the end of war [1]. The proof of the Day lies in deeds: one pure act now outweighs the labor of ages, exile turns into proclamation, and the oneness of humanity moves from promise toward practice in education, cooperation and universal peace. Mark’s seed that outgrows the sower’s understanding [2] and the Qur’an’s foam that passes while lasting benefit remains [3] show how to measure an influence that works quietly. From here the path leads to spiritual springtime, to prophecy and its fulfillment, and to the patient growth of the Cause in particular lives.

order.why: Begin with the Day described as the fulfillment of earlier promises, the opening of a new horizon and an occasion for joy. Follow the images of Sinai, Zion, springtime and festival in their particular scriptural settings. Celebration can coexist with exile and sorrow, and the dawn of a new age need not mean that its possibilities are already fully realized. How does recognition of a promised Day change the meaning of the present? What work remains for those who celebrate it?
shortened: Oh, how I long to announce unto every spot on the surface of the earth, and to carry to each one of its cities, the glad-tidings of this Revelation - a Revelation to which the heart of Sinai hath been attracted, and in whose name the Burning Bush is calling: 'Unto God, the Lord of Lords, belong the kingdoms of earth and heaven.' Verily this is the Day in which both land and sea rejoice at this announcement, the Day for which have been laid up those things which God, through a bounty beyond the ken of mortal mind or heart, hath destined for revelation.

references.label: 2 · Mark 4:26–32 · Seeds, growth and shelter
references.note: Read Mark 4:26–32 in the King James Version. Jesus compares the kingdom of God with seed whose growth exceeds the sower’s understanding and with a small seed that becomes shelter for birds. Compare these images with the collection’s spiritual springtime, planted seeds and gradual spread of influence. What part belongs to human work, and what cannot be controlled or fully understood? How might the shelter a tree provides change the way we assess its greatness? Attend to the different settings and claims of the parables and the Baha’i accounts; resemblance does not make their meanings identical.

references.label: 3 · Qur’an 13:16–18 · Passing foam and lasting benefit
references.note: Read Qur’an 13:16–18 in Dr. Mustafa Khattab’s The Clear Quran, using the surrounding verses shown with verse 17. Rain fills valleys according to their capacity; foam and the residue from working metal pass away, while what benefits people remains. The passage places these comparisons within a contrast between truth and falsehood, with recognition and response to God on either side. Compare the compilation’s explicit use of the foam image and its insistence on deeds that benefit humanity. How could lasting benefit help us distinguish influence from noise or prestige? What can a parable disclose, and what further inquiry does it invite?
